exam: A 45‑year‑old farmer presents with sudden right‑hand weakness and facial droop; what bedside test confirms an upper motor neuron lesion and why? — Perform the Babinski test; an extensor plantar response indicates corticospinal tract involvement.

In a patient with a cervical spinal cord injury, why is loss of pain and temperature sensation contralateral to the side of weakness typical? — Brown‑Séquard syndrome: hemisection damages ipsilateral corticospinal tract and contralateral spinothalamic tract.

How would you differentiate a pyramidal tract lesion from an extrapyramidal one in a patient with gait disturbance? — Look for spasticity and hyperreflexia (pyramidal) versus rigidity without reflex changes (extrapyramidal).

A patient with HIV develops progressive lower limb spasticity; what common tropical infection should be considered and what is the first diagnostic step? — Consider spinal tuberculosis; obtain a chest X‑ray and, if possible, MRI of the spine; if imaging unavailable, perform a thorough neurological exam and start empirical anti‑TB therapy after sputum testing.

Why is a high‑dose corticosteroid not recommended for acute spinal cord compression in low‑resource settings? — Lack of monitoring for infection and hyperglycaemia; supportive care and early decompression are preferred.

During a bedside exam you note a brisk knee reflex but normal ankle reflex; which tract is most likely affected? — Upper motor neuron lesion above the lumbosacral enlargement affecting the corticospinal tract to the knee more than the ankle.

What is the significance of a preserved dorsal column sensation in a patient with motor weakness? — Suggests an anterior cord syndrome sparing posterior columns, often due to vascular compromise of the anterior spinal artery.

A child with sickle cell disease presents with sudden back pain and weakness; what descending pathway injury should you suspect and what urgent test is needed? — Possible spinal infarction of the anterior spinal artery; obtain urgent MRI or, if unavailable, a CT scan and start supportive care.
ai.title: Descending Motor Pathways
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: Descending motor pathways transmit signals from the brain to spinal cord motor neurons, coordinating voluntary and involuntary movements, posture and balance. Understanding their anatomy helps localise lesions in common low‑resource settings.

b: Pyramidal = corticospinal, fast, direct
Extrapyramidal = indirect, modulates tone and gait
sections.p: The brain sends motor commands down the spinal cord via two major systems: the pyramidal (corticospinal) tracts for precise voluntary movement and the extrapyramidal (reticulospinal, vestibulospinal, rubrospinal, tectospinal) tracts for posture, tone and reflex modulation.

b: Lateral corticospinal tract: 85‑90% cross at pyramids
Anterior corticospinal tract: crosses at spinal level
Reticulospinal: originates in reticular formation, bilateral
Vestibulospinal: from vestibular nuclei, ipsilateral
sections.p: Pyramidal fibers originate in the primary motor cortex, descend through the corona radiata, internal capsule, cerebral peduncles and form the lateral and anterior corticospinal tracts in the spinal cord. Extrapyramidal tracts arise from brainstem nuclei and travel in the ventral and lateral funiculi.

b: Lateral CST near dorsal column medial lemniscus
Anterior CST ventral to ventral horn
sections.p: In the spinal cord, corticospinal tracts lie in the lateral funiculus (lateral) and anterior funiculus (anterior). They are adjacent to the dorsal column (sensory) and the ventral horn (motor neurons). Brainstem tracts run alongside cranial nerve nuclei.

b: Anterior spinal artery → ventral CST
Posterior spinal arteries → dorsal aspects
sections.p: Pyramidal tracts receive blood from the anterior spinal artery (ventral) and the posterior spinal arteries (dorsal). Brainstem origins are supplied by the basilar artery and its branches (e.g., anterior inferior cerebellar artery).

b: Upper motor neuron lesions → spasticity, hyperreflexia
Extrapyramidal lesions → rigidity, gait disturbance
sections.p: Motor commands travel via upper motor neurons in the corticospinal tracts to lower motor neurons in the anterior horn. Extrapyramidal tracts modulate lower motor neuron excitability through interneurons.

b: Lateral CST → distal hand/finger dexterity
Anterior CST → trunk flexion/extension
Reticulospinal → startle and locomotor rhythm
sections.p: Pyramidal tracts produce fine, fractionated movements of distal limbs. Extrapyramidal tracts maintain axial tone, posture, balance and coordinate automatic movements such as walking.

b: Cortical stroke → contralateral face and arm weakness, pronator drift
Internal capsule infarct → dense hemiplegia, facial droop
Brown‑Séquard syndrome → ipsilateral UMN signs below lesion, contralateral pain loss
Anterior cord syndrome → loss of motor and pain, preserved dorsal sensation
sections.p: Lesions at different levels produce characteristic patterns useful for bedside localisation, especially when imaging is limited.

t.b: Confirms lesion site; if unavailable, use clinical localisation and CT if possible
Distinguishes UMN vs LMN patterns; guides urgency of imaging
Rule out metabolic mimics of weakness

b: Positive Babinski → UMN lesion
Clonus > 3 beats → corticospinal tract involvement
Spastic gait → pyramidal tract disease
sections.p: Focus on pattern of weakness, presence of spasticity, hyperreflexia, and Babinski sign to differentiate upper from lower motor neuron lesions.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden onset of bilateral weakness suggesting spinal cord compression
Rapidly progressing weakness with respiratory compromise
New onset of flaccid paralysis after trauma
